analysis.one_liner: Bans political action committees from federal elections and cuts individual contribution limits.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for political action committees — the pooled-money committees funded by corporations, unions, and interest groups — to give money or spend on campaigns for federal office. It also would have cut the limit on what an individual can give to a candidate from $1,000 to $500. Candidates would have had to rely on small individual donations instead of PAC money.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters who want candidates to answer to individual constituents rather than to organized money. Candidates without access to PAC networks — challengers, and candidates from districts where big corporate or union PACs are not active — would compete on more level ground.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new section to the Federal Election Campaign Act stating that no person other than an individual or a political committee may contribute, solicit, or spend to influence a federal election, eliminating PAC activity in federal races [S3].
It cuts the cap on individual contributions to a candidate from $1,000 to $500, which would make candidates raise money in smaller amounts from more people [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees — the corporate, union, and interest-group committees that currently channel large pooled sums to federal candidates — lose their entire federal election role. Incumbents who depend on PAC fundraising would have to rebuild their donor bases from individual givers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Political action committees and PAC-dependent incumbents

drawbacks.text: Banning PACs does not stop the underlying money: well-funded interests could redirect spending to independent expenditures and other channels outside candidate committees, which is the strongest good-faith objection to a PAC ban [S3].

Cutting the individual limit to $500 while PAC money disappears could leave candidates — especially challengers who lack wealthy personal networks — with no realistic way to raise the large sums modern campaigns require, potentially making it harder for non-wealthy candidates to run [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem — federal candidates funded through pooled committee money — and its cut to the individual limit pushes toward small-dollar fundraising. But it is a blunt instrument: a PAC ban alone does not prevent organized money from reaching campaigns through independent spending, and halving the individual limit could burden candidates who lack access to large donor networks. Its practical significance is limited by the fact that it never advanced beyond introduction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Oversight Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Glenn Poshard introduced the bill on January 19, 1995, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Oversight [S5].
The House Oversight Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Political action committees and the incumbents who fundraise through them — the system the bill would have dismantled stayed exactly as it was.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PACs and incumbents who rely on them

for.name: Rep. Glenn Poshard
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban PAC activity in federal elections and lower the individual contribution cap.

against.name: House Committee on House Oversight
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 19, 1995 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no Republicans or other Democrats cosponsored the bill, so its support never took a measurable partisan shape; it died in a committee controlled by the new Republican majority.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, union, and interest-group committees)
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated PACs' entire role in federal elections — no contributions, solicitation, or spending. PACs exist to pool money from organized interests and convert it into access and influence with federal officeholders, which is a channel ordinary voters do not control.

A ban on PAC activity and a lower contribution cap would change how campaigns raise money, shrinking the market for PAC-focused fundraising operations while shifting effort toward broader small-donor solicitation.
